plan: [This is a 5-player, third-price sealed-bid auction. For independent uniform values, symmetric equilibrium bidding is b(v) = (n-1)/(n-k+1) * v = 4/3 * v (derivable as the best response). With my value v = 20, the equilibrium bid is 26.666... I round to the nearest $0.1 to maximize long-run expected profit given opponents following the same logic.]

Compute symmetric BNE for a 5-bidder, 3rd-price auction with values U[0,49]. Solving first-order condition yields bidding function s(v)=4/3·v. For v=29 the equilibrium bid is 4/3·29 = 38.666..., so round to the nearest $0.1. This bid maximizes expected surplus assuming opponents use the symmetric strategy.

[I have value $45. With four opponents whose values are uniform on [0,49], bidding more raises my win probability much faster than it raises expected third-price payment. Under truthful-opponent bids the objective ∝ b^4(45−0.4b) is increasing on [0,49], and the chance the third-highest exceeds $45 is negligible. To maximize long-run expected profit I will bid the maximum, \$49.]

[I will bid my true private value, $8. In this 5‑bidder third‑price auction the winner pays the second‑highest opponent bid; bidding my value ensures any win yields non‑negative payoff (the payment cannot exceed my bid). No past rounds to exploit and values redraw each round, so truthful bidding is the safe, profit‑maximizing strategy here.]

[With 5 bidders and third-price payment, the winner pays the 3rd-highest bid. My value ($11) is low vs. the 0–49 range; chance I'm the highest is (11/50)^4 ≈ 0.23%. Overbidding risks winning while paying a third-highest bid that exceeds $11, creating a loss. To maximize expected payoff (and avoid negative outcomes) I should avoid forcing wins when unlikely to be highest. Bid minimally (0) to prevent costly wins while still capturing the tiny upside if others also bid zero.]
